newsitem.title: USA: GM September sales dip, Chrysler sales stay strong.
newsitem.headline: GM September sales dip, Chrysler sales stay strong.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. capped off a record model year Tuesday by reporting robust September U.S. car and truck sales, while General Motors Corp. said its sales for the month declined slightly.

Chrysler's car and truck sales, backed by aggressive incentives, remained surprisingly strong as its total sales rose 22 percent on a daily selling basis to 183,664 vehicles from 157,004 a year earlier. There were 24 selling days in September of this year vs. 25 selling days in the same month last year.
Chrysler said its domestic car sales rose 18.2 percent to 57,070 units, while its domestic truck sales rose 24.4 percent to 125,791 units.

Meanwhile, GM said its car sales fell 10 percent to 226,740 units, which offset a 13 percent gain in truck sales to 150,737 units. On a daily selling-rate basis, GM's total U.S. vehicle sales for September fell 2.1 percent to 377,477 cars and trucks.
"There's no slowdown and there's no boom," Dean Witter Reynolds auto analyst Ronald Glantz said of the GM and Chrysler results.

He estimated that industry sales for the month, when Ford Motor Co. reports on Thursday, will reach a seasonally adjusted annual rate of about 15.1 million cars and light trucks, slightly ahead of last year and about even with the average for July and August.
GM's September totals include 2,873 cars made by Swedish automaker Saab, compared with 2,282 cars a year earlier. GM owns half of Saab.

GM spokesman Dean Rotondo attributed the decline in passenger car sales largely to consumers deciding to wait for many of the 15 new vehicles that the auto giant plans to introduce during the 1997 model year.

Car sales at all of GM's divisions except Saturn fell in September, with Chevrolet car sales off 8.4 percent, Pontiac sales off 4.3 percent, Oldsmobile sales off 30.3 percent, Buick sales off 14.3 percent and Cadillac sales off 4.7 percent. Saturn sales were up 2.5 percent.

"GM's position will be further enhanced by the introduction of more new models during the 1997 model year than in any year in almost two decades," GM Vice President of Marketing Ronald Zarrella said in a statement.
For the 1996 model year ended Sept. 30, GM sold a total of 4,912,544 cars and trucks, a 0.3 percent decline from the 4,928,120 vehicles it sold a year earlier.
Chrysler's model-year sales rose about 12 percent to 2,407,700 vehicles from 2,150,871 in 1995. They surpassed Chrysler's previous record of 2,186,128 cars and trucks, set in the 1994 model year.
James Holden, Chrysler executive vice president of sales and marketing, said the September perfomance "is a good sign that people like our new '97 models and they're buying them."
Helping Chrysler's sales are aggressive rebates and leasing promotions. The automaker has broken with tradition by continuing its 1996 clearance incentives through the start of the 1997 model year.

Deliveries of Cherokee sport utility vehicles, offered on a $199-a-month lease, soared 79 percent during September to 15,207 units. Deliveries of Grand Cherokees, available as low as $299 a month, rose 30 percent to 23,413 units.
Chrysler's minivan sales rose 13 percent, while Dodge Ram pickup truck sales rose 46 percent.
Among Japanese automakers, Nissan Motor Co. Ltd. reported a 2.6 percent increase in September sales to 83,765 units, with domestic car sales up 13.1 percent and domestic truck sales off 2.7 percent.

Subaru, a unit of Fuji Heavy Industries Ltd. reported that its September U.S. sales rose 15.8 percent to 10,864, with sales of U.S.-built Legacy and Outback cars up 16.1 percent. The performance caps Subaru's best quarter since 1990.

Isuzu Motors Ltd.'s total vehicle sales fell 24.2 percent from a year ago, largely because of a sharp drop in Trooper sport utility vehicle sales caused by a Consumer Reports article that alleges the vehicle is prone to tipping over, and also combined with unusually strong sales the month before.
Trooper sales fell to 774 from 4,870 in September 1995. The automaker said it normally sells about 1,400 Troopers a month.
